title: Chapter 263: The Stench
html:
Yang Chen and Li Xue rushed outside. The three students stood together, staring down a corridor filled with darkness.

“Where are the footsteps?”

“I heard them! It sounded as though someone was hopping down the corridor!”

“You’re frightening yourself. Come help us search.”

Li Xue dragged Wang Dan into the final room, while Yang Chen lingered outside. He repeated Wang Dan’s word under his breath. “Hopping?”

The three students ransacked the bedroom. Most of the rubbish covering the beds consisted of foam and wooden blocks. It looked filthy, but none of it could have produced the smell.

“Was this room reserved for rubbish?” Li Xue covered her nose with one sleeve. “But why does that bed have a mattress? Who would sleep in such filth?”

“The former occupant isn’t our immediate concern.” Yang Chen picked up a piece of rubbish and sniffed it. “We noticed the stench as soon as we entered this hidden scenario, and it is strongest here. Whatever produces it must be inside this room. Find the source, and we solve the scenario’s mystery.”

“Yang Chen has a point. The room is full of rubbish, yet none of it smells like this.” Wang Dan approached the only bed with a mattress. “The odor is strongest around the cleanest bed.”

He seized one corner of the mattress and ripped it aside. Nothing horrifying waited beneath it—only a notebook. Wang Dan picked it up and began to read.

“I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have come so close. I only wanted to help you pick up the ball.

“Teacher, I didn’t mean to dirty my shirt. No one bullied me. It was all my fault.

“Father, I will try harder to be good. Please don’t hit me anymore.

“I’m sorry. I don’t know why my smile looks so ugly. I won’t smile again.

“Please tell me what I did wrong. I can change. I really can!

“I only want to be like them. I’m sorry…”

The notebook was thin, but it was filled with apologies.

“What was wrong with him? Why did he apologize for everything? If people bullied him, he should have fought back!” Wang Dan scoffed, contemptuous of what the writer had—or had not—done.

“Look at this.” Li Xue found the pieces of a torn photograph in the wastebasket. She fitted them together until an image emerged. “A father and son, I think.”

The son was dangerously obese, and his shame showed even in the photograph. Frightened of the camera, he hid behind his father. The scowling man had one hand clamped around the boy’s neck, dragging him forward.

“Is this a stepfather?”

Wang Dan opened the notebook for the others. Its early pages seemed ordinary, but the farther they read, the more uncomfortable they became.

The boy’s name never appeared; his classmates called him Piggy. His father, one of Western Jiujiang’s Private Academy’s sponsors, was wealthy and exceptionally harsh. Though the notebook never stated the reason, its entries revealed the truth between the lines: the boy’s mother had betrayed his father, who redirected his resentment toward their son.

The boy yearned for his father’s love, but no degree of obedience earned him anything except beatings and scorn. He lived every moment with care, finding satisfaction only while eating. Food became his sole release from stress, and his weight had already become dangerous in childhood.

The boy’s deteriorating appearance inspired no concern in his father—only the gratification of revenge. Too young to understand, the child ate even more whenever it made his father smile. As he grew, both his body and mind became ill.

At school, the boy withdrew into himself, and no one wanted to sit near him. At home, the smallest mistake invited his father’s fists and feet. Slowly, his heart warped. What others considered beautiful became ugly to him, while the things they fled from became precious.

He was often caught stealing cafeteria leftovers or scavenging from dumpsters. Each incident earned another beating, but he could no longer stop. His understanding of the world had inverted completely.

After several such incidents, one beating grew so severe that the boy was hospitalized and the police became involved. Under pressure from law enforcement, his father finally agreed to move him into the school dormitory.

Because the father sponsored the academy, the school opened a private room for his son. Life in the dormitory forced the boy into closer contact with other students. His apologies multiplied, and his condition grew severe.

Before long, boys in the neighboring rooms noticed a stench. School employees traced it to the private room and forced open the door. The once-clean bedroom overflowed with every kind of rubbish. To the boy, however, the filthy, reeking waste was beautiful decoration.

The school had the room cleaned, punished the boy, and contacted his father. The man responded with the only lesson he knew: another brutal beating. The notebook described that night’s punishment in painful detail. His father did not leave until after midnight.

However unbearable his life became, it continued. The wounds on his body healed; those in his mind only deepened. Soon the stench returned to the dormitory corridor. The school was unwilling to expel the son of a major sponsor.

No matter how often the room was cleaned, the boy never changed. Eventually, the school emptied the neighboring rooms and assigned someone to clear his bedroom every few days.

Days became weeks, and the stench seemed to permeate the floor and walls.

By then, Western Jiujiang’s Private Academy was preoccupied with the ‘accidents’ in the girls’ dormitory. No one had time for the boy. Even the cleaners stopped visiting.

The broken boy continued carrying rubbish into his room, and the stench thickened.

From that point onward, the diary repeated a single theme: apologies to his father and pleas for forgiveness.
